lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Part 3. You will hear two education students, Zara and Tom, discussing a presentation they are preparing on school buildings of the future. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 23.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Tom, have you had a chance to read the brief for our presentation on school buildings of the future?

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Yes, last night. My only worry is that fifteen minutes isn't very long for a topic like that.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Really? I think it's plenty, as long as we plan it carefully. What bothered me was whether we have to do our own research, like interviewing teachers or visiting schools.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: No, I asked Dr Evans about that. She said it's fine to use published sources, as long as we evaluate them properly.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Oh, good. But she also said we have to show real examples, with photos and floor plans of actual schools, not just describe ideas in general.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: I know, and that worries me too. Good pictures of the inside of schools are surprisingly hard to find, because schools are careful about privacy.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Exactly. That's going to take us ages.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Well, let's start by deciding what kind of school we're going to focus on. I was thinking of primary schools. There's so much interesting design for young children.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Mm, but Sam's group is doing primary schools, and Dr Evans doesn't want two groups covering the same thing.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Fair enough. What about colleges for adults, then? Lots of people go back to study later in life these days.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: I thought about that, but I couldn't find much written about it. Secondary schools have far more research behind them, and teenagers have quite specific needs.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: OK, you've convinced me. Let's go with secondary.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Right. Next, we need to say what the main challenge for these buildings will be. I'd assumed it would be space, with pupil numbers going up.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Actually, the figures I saw for our region suggest that numbers will stay about the same for the next ten years.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Really? Then what about the cost of repairing old buildings? Lots of schools round here were built in the nineteen-sixties.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: That's a real problem, but it's more about funding than design, and our topic is design.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: True. So it's heat, then. My cousin's a teacher, and she says her classroom is already too hot to work in by June.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Yes. Summers are getting hotter, so I agree that keeping classrooms cool is going to be the biggest issue.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 24 to 30.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: So, let's go through the developments we want to include. First, outdoor classrooms. A lot of new schools have covered areas outside where lessons can take place.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: I like that. A school in the countryside has fields around it anyway. But for children in the middle of a city, it might be the only time they spend outdoors all day.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: That's true. And they're not expensive to build, either.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Then there's furniture on wheels, so desks and chairs can be pushed around easily.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Some teachers say that makes the classroom noisy.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Maybe, but you can turn rows of desks into groups in a few seconds, so pupils can do projects with each other much more easily.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Yes, I think that's the main advantage. What about natural light? Some designs have huge windows and skylights in the roof.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: People do say pupils just stare out of the window.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Possibly, but the big gain is that the school would hardly need to switch the lights on during the day, which would really cut its electricity costs.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Agreed, as long as there are good blinds for the summer. One design I read about has a touch screen built into every desk.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Hmm. I imagine a lot of parents would love the idea, but I'm not sure. Children would be tempted to play games or send messages instead of listening to the teacher.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: That's my worry too. It would be really hard to keep them concentrating.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Another idea is to build the sports hall and the library with their own entrance, so they can be opened in the evenings and at weekends.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: That's clever. Then people who live nearby could use them for clubs and classes, instead of the rooms sitting empty.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: There'd be a bit of extra cleaning, but that wouldn't cost much.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: What about open-plan schools, with large shared areas instead of separate classrooms?

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: They were popular for a while. For a subject like art, where pupils move around and work on big projects, they're great. But you can't really teach music or a language in a space like that, because of the noise.

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Last one, then: sensors that measure the air in each room and open the windows when it gets stuffy.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Aren't they very expensive?

lines.speaker: ZARA
lines.text: Not any more. And fresh air keeps everyone alert, the staff as much as the children. Teachers get tired by the afternoon too, you know.

lines.speaker: TOM
lines.text: Good point. Right, shall we divide up the reading?

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: That is the end of Part 3.

items.text: sports halls and libraries with a separate entrance

evidence.quote: I know, and that worries me too

pairs: Good pictures of the inside of schools are surprisingly hard to find
21.why: Zara says they must show photos and floor plans of real schools. Tom says 'that worries me too', so they are both worried about finding pictures.
21.trap: Tom worries about the length (A), but Zara does not. Zara worries about research (B), but Tom says published sources are fine. Only C worries both of them.

evidence.quote: Secondary schools have far more research behind them, and teenagers have quite specific needs

22.why: Zara suggests secondary schools, which are for teenagers, and Tom agrees: 'Let's go with secondary.'
22.trap: Primary schools (A) are rejected because another group is doing them. Adult colleges (C) are rejected because there is not much written about them.

evidence.quote: keeping classrooms cool is going to be the biggest issue

pairs: keeping classrooms at a comfortable temperature
23.why: Both students agree that hotter summers make keeping classrooms cool the biggest issue.
23.trap: Space for more pupils (B) is Zara's first idea, but Tom says numbers will stay the same. Repairs (C) are a funding problem, not a design one, so they drop it.

evidence.quote: for children in the middle of a city, it might be the only time they spend outdoors all day

pairs: particularly useful for pupils in city schools
for children in the middle of a city
24.why: Country schools already have fields, but for city children an outdoor classroom may be their only time outside. So it is especially useful in city schools.
24.trap: Tom says they are 'not expensive to build', so H (expensive) is wrong.

evidence.quote: so pupils can do projects with each other much more easily

25.why: Desks on wheels can be moved into groups quickly, so pupils can do projects with each other. That means working together.
25.trap: Some teachers say it is noisy, but Zara answers 'Maybe, but…' and gives the main advantage.

evidence.quote: which would really cut its electricity costs

26.why: With big windows and skylights, the school would not need lights in the day, so electricity costs go down.
26.trap: 'Stare out of the window' sounds like E (distract pupils), but Tom answers 'Possibly, but the big gain is…'. E is the answer for the touch screens.

evidence.quote: Children would be tempted to play games or send messages instead of listening to the teacher

pairs: tempted to play games or send messages instead of listening
27.why: Both students think children would play games or send messages instead of listening. This means the screens would distract them.
27.trap: Parents are mentioned, but Tom thinks parents would love the idea. So C (unpopular with parents) is wrong.

evidence.quote: people who live nearby could use them for clubs and classes

pairs: could use them for clubs and classes
28.why: With a separate entrance, local people could use the sports hall and library in the evenings and at weekends.
28.trap: Extra cleaning is mentioned, but 'that wouldn't cost much', so H is wrong.

evidence.quote: For a subject like art, where pupils move around and work on big projects, they're great

pairs: suit some subjects better than others
For a subject like art … they're great. But you can't really teach music or a language
29.why: Tom says open-plan areas are great for art but bad for music and languages because of the noise. So they suit some subjects better than others.

evidence.quote: the staff as much as the children

pairs: the staff as much as the children
30.why: Fresh air keeps everyone alert, the staff as much as the children. So the sensors help teachers as well as pupils.
30.trap: Tom asks if the sensors are expensive, but Zara says 'Not any more', so H is wrong.
